title: Permutations
corePattern: Backtracking with DFS and State Restoration
interviewTips: Clarify: Are all numbers distinct? Yes per constraints - ask how duplicates would change it (would need sorting + skip logic like Permutations II).
Trade-off: Used-array version is clearer to explain, swap in-place version saves O(n) extra space and avoids path copying overhead - mention both.
Edge-case tip: Always copy path when adding to result (path[:] / new ArrayList<>(path)) otherwise all entries reference same mutable list.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Backtracking with Used Array
approaches.intuition: Build permutation one position at a time. At each step try every number that has not been used yet, mark it used, recurse, then unmark it to try the next choice.
approaches.theory: This is DFS over a decision tree of depth n. Level d corresponds to position d in permutation. Branching factor shrinks from n to 1. Each root-to-leaf path is one permutation. Used boolean array tracks which indices are already in current path. Backtracking (undo choice) restores state so sibling branches start clean. Total leaves = n! .

timeComplexity.explanation: There are n! permutations. For each we do O(n) work to build path and O(n) to copy it into result. Number of recursive calls is sum_{k=0..n} P(n,k) which is bounded by O(n * n!).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output stores n! lists of length n. Auxiliary space is O(n) for path + O(n) for used array + O(n) recursion stack depth.

steps: from [1] try 2 -> path=[1,2] -> try 3 -> path=[1,2,3] => save [1,2,3], backtrack
from [1] try 3 -> path=[1,3] -> try 2 -> path=[1,3,2] => save [1,3,2], backtrack
pop to [] try 2 -> path=[2] expands to [2,1,3], [2,3,1]
pop to [] try 3 -> path=[3] expands to [3,1,2], [3,2,1]

edgeCases: n=1: single element returns [[1]] - base case start==len works
Empty path copy bug: must append copy not reference
All distinct guaranteed so no dedup needed

approaches.name: Approach 2: In-Place Swap Backtracking
approaches.intuition: Fix prefix nums[0:start] as already permuted, then swap each candidate into position start to choose what goes next. Recurse to fix next position, then swap back.
approaches.theory: Partition array into fixed prefix [0,start) and remaining suffix [start,n). Loop i from start to n-1 swaps nums[start] with nums[i] to place every remaining element at position start exactly once. Recurse with start+1. When start==n, current array order is one permutation. Swap-back restores original order for next sibling. No used array or extra path needed, operates directly on input array.

timeComplexity.explanation: Same n! leaves, each leaf costs O(n) to copy array into result. Swaps are O(1). Time is asymptotically optimal because output size itself is O(n * n!).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output dominates. Auxiliary space is O(n) recursion stack only, no used or path arrays - O(1) extra excluding output and stack.

steps: start=1: i=1 swap(1,1) => [1,2,3], recurse start=2: i=2 => [1,2,3] save; i=2 swap(2,2) variant [1,3,2] save after swap(1,2)
back to start=0: i=1 swap(0,1) => [2,1,3], recurse yields [2,1,3], [2,3,1]
back to start=0: i=2 swap(0,2) => [3,2,1], recurse yields [3,2,1], [3,1,2]

edgeCases: n=1: loop runs once, start==1 saves copy
Must swap back after recursion else array stays mutated for next i
Must copy nums when saving (nums[:] / new list) because later swaps mutate it
